add_eyes.name: George Weller
add_eyes.role: War correspondent for the Chicago Daily News, aged 38; Pulitzer Prize winner (1943)
add_eyes.where: Nagasaki, from 6 September 1945; then Allied POW camps in Kyushu
add_eyes.authenticity: Dispatches written in Nagasaki in September 1945 and sent to MacArthur's censors in Tokyo, who suppressed them. After Weller died in 2002, his son Anthony found the carbon copies among his papers. Mainichi Shimbun printed four of them on 17 June 2005, and the full set appeared as First into Nagasaki (2006). These are dated press dispatches, not a private diary, but they were written in the city at the time. The account of the POW camps comes from the same set.
add_eyes.bio: Weller slipped into southern Japan without permission and reached Nagasaki about four weeks after the bomb, before any other foreign reporter. His first dispatch defended the bombing. Within hours his reports turned to hospital wards where people with no visible wounds were dying of an illness the doctors could not name.

sources.title: Asia-Pacific Journal: First into Nagasaki, Weller's censored dispatches
Columbia Journalism Review on the recovered Weller dispatches
CBS News: Censored A-bomb dispatches printed

add_eyes.name: Nagai Takashi
add_eyes.role: Radiologist and lecturer at Nagasaki Medical College, aged 37; head of the college's 11th Medical Relief Team
add_eyes.where: Radium Room, Nagasaki Medical College, Urakami; from 12 August a relief station at Mitsuyama, north-east of the city
add_eyes.vantage_label: victim and physician near the hypocentre
add_eyes.authenticity: Nagasaki ika daigaku genshi bakudan kyūgo hōkoku, a report to the college president on the team's work from 9 August to 8 October 1945. The original is held by Nagasaki University's Atomic Bomb Disease Institute. It was published in 1970 (Asahi Shinbunsha), and an English translation, Atomic Bomb Rescue and Relief Report, came out in 2000 (NASHIM, Nagasaki). The exact date of writing was not confirmed this session. It was written after the relief station closed in October 1945, so it is a close-to-the-event report, not a daily diary.
add_eyes.bio: Nagai was a radiologist who already had leukaemia from his work. The blast caught him at his desk and cut an artery in his head. His wife died at their home in Urakami. He kept treating patients for three days in the ruins, then led his surviving staff to Mitsuyama, where for 58 days they treated people for symptoms that he, as a radiation specialist, was among the first to recognise. His later books, such as The Bells of Nagasaki, made him the city's best-known witness.

sources.title: LinguaHiroshima: Atomic Bomb Rescue and Relief Report (bibliographic record)
Extracts from Dr Takashi Nagai's first report (La Radioactivité)
Japan Radioisotope Association: medical history note citing the report (PDF)

add_eyes.name: Kobayashi Jirō
add_eyes.role: Secretary-General of the House of Peers, aged 54
add_eyes.vantage_label: inside the Diet, hearing the cabinet's news
add_eyes.authenticity: Kobayashi Jirō papers, Modern Japanese Political History Materials Room, National Diet Library. The 1945 diary is digitised in the NDL Digital Collections, and its 11 and 15 August entries are shown in the NDL online exhibition 'The World of Diaries'.
add_eyes.bio: Kobayashi ran the upper house's secretariat, as Ōki Misao ran the lower house's, and the two diaries make a matched pair. His August entries track Japan's surrender offer moving through neutral capitals, the celebrations reported from Chongqing and Okinawa, and the official world's private reckoning when the Emperor spoke.

sources.title: NDL, 'The World of Diaries': Kobayashi Jirō

add_eyes.name: Alexander John James
add_eyes.role: British prisoner of war held by the Japanese
add_eyes.vantage_label: prisoner in Japan's empire, outside the home islands
add_eyes.authenticity: Daily notebook diary, transcribed online by the Far Eastern Heroes site from the original. The original manuscript was not examined this session. Entries are written day by day and include practical details, such as supply drops and a woman killed by a falling drum, that suggest they were written at the time.
add_eyes.bio: James was held in Seoul, then the colonial capital Keijō. He heard of the surrender from a milkman before the guards announced it. His notebook follows the strange interval of late August, when prisoners waited under their former captors' guard while B-29s dropped food and Soviet airmen turned up, until the day of the formal signing.

sources.title: Far Eastern Heroes: A. J. James diary, 15 August – 10 November 1945

add_eyes.name: Salvador H. Laurel
add_eyes.role: Son of President José P. Laurel of the Japanese-sponsored Philippine Republic, aged 16; later Vice President of the Philippines
add_eyes.where: Nara, where the Laurel family had been evacuated
add_eyes.vantage_label: teenage exile in the old capital
add_eyes.authenticity: Wartime diary published by the Philippine Diary Project. The entry used here was cited and summarised in Manuel L. Quezon III's 2020 essay on three Filipino diarists of Japan's fall.
add_eyes.bio: When the Philippine puppet government fled before MacArthur's return, the teenage Laurel went with it into exile in Japan. In Nara he saw defeat from a Japanese neighbourhood, as a guest of the losing side who was about to become a subject of the winning one.

sources.title: Manuel L. Quezon III, 'WWII and the Fall of Japan, in the Eyes of Three Filipinos'
Philippine Diary Project: Salvador H. Laurel, 15 August 1945

add_entries.headline: Health minister brings word: Hiroshima destroyed by one bomb
add_entries.digest: Just after noon, Health Minister Okada calls on Ōki with news from Hiroshima. A single bomb, dropped by parachute and set to burst a few hundred metres above the ground, fell at about 8:30 the previous morning and flattened and burned an area four kilometres across. Casualties are reported at well over a hundred thousand. The regional governor is dead, while Field Marshal Hata survived. Ōki writes simply that this is a terrible business.
add_entries.source_note: NDL online exhibition 'The World of Diaries', Ōki Misao page, entry of 7 August 1945 (image ookim_19450807).

add_entries.headline: News of Nagasaki, and useless official advice on the bomb
add_entries.digest: Guerrero records the news that a second city, Nagasaki, has been hit by the new bomb. He scorns the official advice telling civilians how to protect themselves against it, which he finds hopelessly inadequate to what the papers have already admitted about Hiroshima.
add_entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project entry of 9 August 1945, as linked and summarised in Manuel L. Quezon III's 2020 essay (quezon.ph). Full entry not fetched directly; the site blocked it.

add_entries.headline: The war minister: we cannot win, but no unconditional surrender
add_entries.digest: Ōki writes down War Minister Anami's position as it has reached him. Anami says the army will obey the nation's decision and admits that, with disarmament looming, the Soviet Union in the war and the atomic bomb, victory is plainly out of reach. Even so, he says the army cannot accept unconditional surrender and is confident one last battle could inflict a heavy blow on the Americans and British.
add_entries.source_note: NDL 'The World of Diaries', Ōki Misao page, entry of 10 August 1945 (image ookim_19450810).

add_entries.headline: Firecrackers in Chongqing; will the Allies take the offer?
add_entries.digest: At 5 p.m. a Foreign Ministry contact, Kase, tells Kobayashi that Japan's conditional acceptance, sent through Sweden and Switzerland on the 10th, has reached the four Allied capitals. Kobayashi notes reports of firecrackers in Chongqing and sirens and gunfire on Okinawa as the Allies celebrate. He guesses that Britain and the United States will accept and that Chiang will not object, but Moscow is the unknown. If the Soviets refuse, the war goes on.
add_entries.source_note: NDL 'The World of Diaries', Kobayashi Jirō page, entry of 11 August 1945 (image kobayas_19450811).

add_entries.headline: A wounded radiologist sets up a clinic in the hills
add_entries.digest: After three days treating victims in the ruins of the college, Nagai leads what is left of his team out of Urakami on foot on the morning of 12 August. They open a relief station at Mitsuyama and see their first patients about 4 p.m. They are exhausted, sick themselves, and have no surgical supplies, so for the worst cases they can give only water and food. Over 58 days they treat 125 bomb patients, and nearly a quarter of them die. Nagai's report describes the burns, the wounds and the new sickness, and suggests treatments for it.
add_entries.source_note: Atomic Bomb Rescue and Relief Report (Eng. trans. 2000), extracts on La Radioactivité; JRIA note for the figures (58 days, 125 patients, 23% mortality); Nagai Memorial Museum chronology. Exact writing date of the report not confirmed.

add_entries.place: Budget Committee room, National Diet Building
add_entries.headline: Tears of grief and rage at the Diet's radio
add_entries.digest: At noon, Ōki gathers with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, the whole staff and the members present in the Budget Committee room to hear the broadcast. As the rescript is read, he bows his head and cannot hold back tears of grief and indignation. He closes the entry by vowing that this bitterness will one day be avenged. In the parliament building, defeat was received as a wound, not a release.
add_entries.source_note: NDL 'The World of Diaries', Ōki Misao page, entry of 15 August 1945 (image ookim_19450815).

add_entries.headline: Awed by the broadcast; the guilty should blame themselves
add_entries.digest: Kobayashi listens to the noon broadcast with a handful of colleagues from the House of Peers secretariat. He writes that he is overcome with awe, and that those responsible for the war must surely be feeling deep self-reproach. In the same building on the same day, his lower-house counterpart Ōki wept with rage.
add_entries.source_note: NDL 'The World of Diaries', Kobayashi Jirō page, entry of 15 August 1945 (image kobayas_19450815).

add_entries.place: A hotel outside Tokyo, then the train to Tokyo
add_entries.headline: Hearing the Emperor among Japanese hotel staff and guests
add_entries.digest: Guerrero hears the broadcast in a hotel alongside its Japanese staff and guests and watches how they take it. Afterwards he rides a tense train back into Tokyo among people who have just learned that their country has lost. As a servant of Japan's client government, he loses with them.
add_entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project entry of 15 August 1945, as summarised in Quezon III's 2020 essay. Hotel location not confirmed.

add_entries.headline: A poem for defeat; chanting from Japanese houses
add_entries.digest: The sixteen-year-old Laurel learns of the surrender from his brother and writes a poem about it. That evening he hears Japanese men chanting inside the houses around them. His cousin tells him it may be preparation for ritual suicide. For the exiled family, Japan's defeat is their own as well.
add_entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project, Salvador H. Laurel, 15 August 1945, as summarised in Quezon III's 2020 essay.

add_entries.headline: The milkman brings the news before the guards do
add_entries.digest: James first hears of Japan's surrender from the milkman and from the radio. Only later does a sentry formally announce it inside the camp. The next day, Koreans celebrate openly in the streets around the camp, and newly freed Allied airmen begin to arrive.
add_entries.source_note: A. J. James diary transcription, Far Eastern Heroes, entries of 15–16 August 1945.

add_entries.headline: Calm on the surface, plots underneath
add_entries.digest: A day after the broadcast, Guerrero writes that the first impression of calm is fading. Tokyo is full of rumours, plots and counter-plots. Ordinary Japanese say almost nothing, and he thinks they are partly stunned, as if hit on the head, and partly going through the motions of daily life.
add_entries.source_note: Philippine Diary Project, entry of 16 August 1945 (fetched directly).

add_entries.headline: B-29s drop food; a falling drum kills a woman
add_entries.digest: Two B-29s fly over and drop supply drums to the prisoners. Most burst on landing, and one kills a local woman. That evening a fellow prisoner, Roger Piggot, dies. Liberation arrives from the air as both a gift and a hazard, and too late for some.
add_entries.source_note: A. J. James diary transcription, Far Eastern Heroes, entry of 29 August 1945.

add_entries.headline: Peace signed: the diarist is a prisoner no longer
add_entries.digest: On the day the surrender is signed in Tokyo Bay, James notes that peace is official and that he is no longer a prisoner. The camp's new etiquette is odd: Allied and Japanese personnel are to salute each other's seniors, the two sides parade in separate lines with speeches and handshakes, and the sentries withdraw from inside the wire. That night there is a party at the Soviet consulate.
add_entries.source_note: A. J. James diary transcription, Far Eastern Heroes, entry of 2 September 1945.

add_entries.headline: First dispatch calls the bombing proper; by evening, doubts
add_entries.digest: In his first dispatch from Nagasaki, Weller describes the bombing as selective and justified, aimed at the city's war plants. He notes that his Japanese guide seems to want him to write it up as an American atrocity. After a day touring the wrecked Urakami valley and its hospitals, his later dispatch is uneasy. He describes survivors dying with no visible wounds, dark mouths and children losing their hair.
add_entries.source_note: Columbia Journalism Review on the recovered dispatches (first filed 8 September 1945); Asia-Pacific Journal excerpt.

add_entries.headline: Hospitals losing patients to an undiagnosed sickness
add_entries.digest: Writing after midnight, Weller reports that the city's hospitals are still losing patients to a strange effect of the bomb. People who thought they had escaped are dying weeks later. The doctors have modern drugs but admit they cannot identify the illness, so they cannot treat it. He calls it 'Disease X', and his last dispatch notes that Japanese doctors are hoping the American scientists arriving on 11 September will know what to do.
add_entries.source_note: Asia-Pacific Journal (dispatch 8, headed 9 September, 1 a.m.); CJR for 'Disease X' and the 11 September team.

add_convergences.label: Surrender signed aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay
add_convergences.note: Still a thin cluster. No diarist here was aboard the Missouri. A British prisoner in Seoul records the signing as the moment he stopped being a POW, while Guerrero, held with Axis diplomats at Atami, is himself in custody. The ceremony is seen only at second hand, from the edges of Japan's former empire.

add_ties.note: Secretaries-general of the two houses of the Imperial Diet, working in the same building. Their 15 August entries record the same broadcast heard a few corridors apart, one in rage and one in awe.
In September, Weller in Nagasaki and Hachiya in Hiroshima were describing the same unexplained deaths of people without wounds, the sickness later identified as radiation illness.
Colleagues at Nagasaki Medical College. Nagai was there on 9 August and wrote up the relief work that autumn, and Wakahara, who was away, reconstructed the losses ten years later.
Both were in Japan with the exiled Laurel government of the Philippines, and the Philippine Diary Project publishes both diaries for the same days.

fix.headline: 'Bear the unbearable' through static, then cold rage
fix.digest: Hachiya joins the staff gathered around a radio in the Communications Bureau. Through the static he catches only the phrase about bearing the unbearable. Then the bureau chief tells them that the Emperor has announced defeat and that they should stay at their posts. Hachiya had expected a call to fight on. His vision blurs, his teeth chatter, he breaks into a cold sweat, and he feels a silent fury at the army. Someone in the room shouts an insult at Tōjō.
fix.source_note: Hiroshima Diary, entry of 15 August 1945, quoted in an excerpt from Wilfred Burchett's Shadows of Hiroshima (Verso Books blog).

updates.why: Verified the 15 August entry from the block quotes in the Verso excerpt. The reactions are those of office staff in the Communications Bureau, not hospital patients, so the earlier digest was wrong.

fix.note: Two Kamakura neighbours hear the broadcast under the same sun, one in glare and cicadas, the other with a tofu seller's confusion. Tanizaki cannot hear it at all, Kafū is on a train and celebrates, and Yamada denies it and then weeps. In Hiroshima, Hachiya catches one phrase through static and shakes with anger at the army. In the Diet building, Ōki weeps with rage and vows revenge while Kobayashi, down the corridor, writes of awe and of the guilty men's shame. Outside the Japanese, Guerrero watches hotel staff take the news, the young Laurel hears chanting in Nara, and in Seoul a British prisoner gets the news from the milkman. Nobody hears the same broadcast in the same way.

updates.why: Added the five new 15 August voices and corrected the Hachiya detail (office staff, not patients).

fix.note: Still the thinnest cluster, though less so now. In Tokyo, Guerrero hears of Nagasaki and scoffs at official advice, Ōki records the war minister admitting the war is lost while refusing to surrender, and Kobayashi watches the surrender offer cross neutral capitals. In Washington, Wallace records Truman's halt. From Nagasaki itself there is still no diary written on the day. The city's own voices come later, in Nagai's relief report that autumn, Weller's censored dispatches in September and Wakahara's reconstruction ten years on.

updates.why: Added the newly verified Tokyo entries for 9–11 August. A Nagasaki diary written in August 1945 still could not be found.

fix.name: Ōki Misao
fix.authenticity: Ōki Misao papers, National Diet Library: pocket notebooks plus ten volumes of official 'Chief Secretary's notes' for 1940–1945. Published by Asahi Shimbunsha in 1969 as Ōki nikki: shūsenji no Teikoku Gikai. The NDL also holds 'Ōki's account of the war devastation of 16 May – 8 June and 14 July 1945', with an entry dated 26 May 1945. Entries for 7, 10 and 15 August 1945 are shown in the NDL online exhibition 'The World of Diaries'.

sources.title: National Diet Library, Modern Japan in archives: the Diet building bombed
NDL, 'The World of Diaries': Ōki Misao

updates.why: The NDL exhibition gives the name as 大木操 (Ōki, with a long vowel), the diary's form (notebooks plus official notes) and the 1969 Asahi edition, and shows the August 1945 entries.
